messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Claire, a 28-year-old third-grade teacher, came to therapy nearly a year after the stalking began, though the acute phase had ended six months prior. It started subtly. A parent of a former student, Michael, began showing up at her classroom door. At first, it was just frequent requests for updates on his son's progress, long after the school year had ended. Then came the notes on her car—"You looked beautiful today, Ms. Claire." The school administration got involved, but he hadn't technically broken any laws. The police were called, and an officer took a report, but they explained their hands were tied until he made a "credible threat." The memory of sitting in the police station, the fluorescent lights harsh overhead, trying to explain her rising dread while the officer nodded sympathetically but did little, was as vivid as the stalking itself. The calls began next. He would breathe heavily into the phone. Just a low, rhythmic, rasping breath. She can still feel the cold plastic of the phone against her ear, the way the world would narrow to that single, horrifying sound. The climax happened on a Tuesday night. She was alone, grading papers. The silence in the house was deafening. She heard a scraping sound at the back door. She froze, a wave of pure horror washing over her. She called 911, and this time, they found him on her porch. He was arrested. But for Claire, the nightmare was just beginning.

She returned to teaching, but she wasn't the same. The heavy breathing of a child who had just sprinted in from recess would send a bolt of ice through her chest, making her lose her train of thought midsentence. She had to leave her classroom door open; a closed door felt like a trap, but an open one allowed anyone to slip in. She became hyper-observant of strangers near the school. A parent lingering too long in the pickup line would trigger a cold sweat. Unusual silence in her classroom—the moment right after she asked for quiet—now felt less like calm and more like a held breath before an attack. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that everyone—the friendly mailman, the new substitute teacher—was a potential threat waiting for an unguarded moment. She felt, in her bones, that she had to be on guard all the time. The cost was immense. She stopped going to the grocery store alone. She stopped having her partner, David, surprise her. He now texts her before entering their own home. She knows it frustrates him, that he feels she doesn't trust him, but she is too terrified to stop the protocols. She can't explain it to him. When he asks what happened, what it felt like, she goes blank. She knows what happened to her—she can feel the fragments: the key in the lock, the taste of fear, the silence on the phone—but the words to string them into a coherent narrative dissolve in her throat. It feels like her life has been destroyed. The person she was before—the one who loved her job, who was trusting and open—is gone.

What finally brought her in was not the fear, but the exhaustion. She was sleeping three hours a night, her body braced for a sound, a breath, a footstep. She had started snapping at her third-graders when they asked too many questions, because the noise felt overwhelming and she needed to listen for danger. She saw the hurt in their faces, and the shame was crushing. She is hoping to find a way to live without this armor. But she is terrified of what it might mean to put it down. She is certain that if she stops watching, he, or someone like him, will be right there.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Triggers: Being Followed: The vignette does not describe the patient feeling followed or tracked, only threat from strangers.
- Memory: Sudden Pieces: The vignette mentions fragments of memory but does not describe them appearing suddenly without warning and then disappearing.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

Claire, a 28-year-old third-grade teacher, came to therapy nearly a year after the stalking began, though the acute phase had ended six months prior. It started subtly. A parent of a former student, Michael, began showing up at her classroom door. At first, it was just frequent requests for updates on his son's progress, long after the school year had ended. Then came the notes on her car—"You looked beautiful today, Ms. Claire." The school administration got involved, but he hadn't technically broken any laws. The police were called, and an officer took a report, but they explained their hands were tied until he made a "credible threat." The memory of sitting in the police station, the fluorescent lights harsh overhead, trying to explain her rising dread while the officer nodded sympathetically but did little, was as vivid as the stalking itself. The calls began next. He would breathe heavily into the phone. Just a low, rhythmic, rasping breath. She can still feel the cold plastic of the phone against her ear, the way the world would narrow to that single, horrifying sound. The climax happened on a Tuesday night. She was alone, grading papers. The silence in the house was deafening. She heard a scraping sound at the back door. She froze, a wave of pure horror washing over her. She called 911, and this time, they found him on her porch. He was arrested. But for Claire, the nightmare was just beginning.

After the arrest, she thought the threat was over, but then she started feeling followed. Walking from her car to the school entrance, she would glance back and see no one, yet the sensation of someone matching her pace, staying just out of sight, would grip her spine. Driving home, she would check her rearview mirror obsessively, certain the same gray sedan was two cars behind, even though it never was. She stopped taking the same route twice. At the grocery store—until she stopped going completely—she would pick up a cart, then abandon it, convinced the man in the produce aisle was tracking her movements with his eyes. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that everyone—the friendly mailman, the new substitute teacher—was a potential threat waiting for an unguarded moment. She felt, in her bones, that she had to be on guard all the time.

What she could not control were the sudden pieces. Without any warning, in the middle of a sentence or while brushing her teeth, a fragment would burst into her mind: the key turning in the lock, the sound of his breathing, the cold plastic of the phone, the sharp taste of fear at the back of her throat. These pieces appeared fully formed, almost like a hallucination, and then vanished just as quickly, leaving her disoriented. She would try to hold onto them, to make sense of the whole story, but they dissolved into mist. When her partner, David, asked what happened, what it felt like, she went blank. She knew the fragments existed but could not string them into a coherent narrative. The heavy breathing of a child who had just sprinted in from recess would trigger one of those pieces—a lightning flash of the phone call—and she would lose her train of thought midsentence. She had to leave her classroom door open; a closed door felt like a trap, but an open one allowed anyone to slip in. Unusual silence in her classroom—the moment right after she asked for quiet—now felt less like calm and more like a held breath before an attack.

The cost was immense. She stopped going to the grocery store alone. She stopped having David surprise her. He now texts her before entering their own home. She knows it frustrates him, that he feels she doesn't trust him, but she is too terrified to stop the protocols. For a while, she managed by sheer will—monitoring hallways, scanning the parking lot, flinching at every unexpected step behind her. But the vigilance wore her down. She was sleeping three hours a night, her body braced for a sound, a breath, a footstep. She had started snapping at her third-graders when they asked too many questions, because the noise felt overwhelming and she needed to listen for danger. She saw the hurt in their faces, and the shame was crushing.

What finally brought her in was not the fear, but the exhaustion. She is hoping to find a way to live without this armor. But she is terrified of what it might mean to put it down. She is certain that if she stops watching, he, or someone like him, will be right there, following her—and the sudden pieces will come back, and she will not be able to protect herself.
